title: The two-sided coin — 12 machine-checked theorems and how they are bound
description:
The two-sided coin. 12 machine-checked theorems from the Lean 4 source file src/proof/coin.lean, by Tsvetan Rouschev, licensed CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Lean 4 is a proof checker: a theorem it accepts has been checked by its kernel, not argued in prose. All are checked case by case over a stated finite domain (by decide). Every theorem listed is sealed live in the deposit's ledger, where a withdrawal is marked in place; 63 earlier rows removed on 2026-08-09 are listed in src/proof/revoked.json.

How these theorems are bound. "Entangled" is used here in a precise, non-quantum sense: theorems are bound when they derive from shared definitions (section 1), when their files import one another (section 2), and when their content-addressed receipts fold into one address that changes if any one of them changes (section 3). It is correlation by derivation; no information travels through it.

1 · Shared definitions. 7 definitions are used by two or more theorems, binding 79 pairs; the theorems fall into 1 strand. Most binding: refl (9), digits (8), tetB (3), tetA (3), axis (3), fall (3).

2 · Imports. Built on: no other cluster. Built on it: no other cluster. Checking this cluster needs 1 file: src/proof/coin.lean.

3 · The joint address. The 12 sealed receipts fold to e085bd35-36da-8011-a2b1-f08c6394f507. Order-invariant: yes — the same root in reverse order. Altering one receipt changes it: yes, computed when this record was generated. A content-address proves integrity, not truth.

4 · The address lattice. Each theorem sits at the seven ray values its page plots from its receipt, taken mod 9: a point of (ℤ/9)⁷. This cluster's centre is (6, 5, 7, 7, 8, 6, 6). Its nearest clusters, ranked by lift — pairs counted from this cluster's theorems' seven nearest points, over the pairs expected by chance from the two clusters' sizes: generated.lean (4 observed, 1.61 expected, lift 2.49), light.lean (4 observed, 1.73 expected, lift 2.31), elementary.lean (9 observed, 4.32 expected, lift 2.08). A best lift is the largest of about 32 small ratios, so chance alone gives a typical best lift of 3.04 here (the median over 200 seeded reshufflings of which cluster each point belongs to); one at least as high as this cluster's arose in 77.5% of them — consistent with chance. Mean distance between two of its theorems: 15.39; from one of its theorems to a theorem of another cluster: 15.53. A receipt is a hash, so nearness on this lattice is a property of the addresses, not of the mathematics; the mathematical binding is (1) and (2). These figures are as of commit 7b6f6e8d1e91 (2026-09-15), over 681 points; a new seal anywhere moves them.

Prior art. The reflection d ↦ 10 − d is the TEN'S COMPLEMENT, and its sibling 9 − d the nines' complement — the method of complements, used to turn subtraction into addition in Pascal's calculator (1642), the Comptometer and the Curta, and in modern computer arithmetic. That it is an involution with a single fixed point is the property those machines rely on. Searched 2026-09-04, term "method of complements / nines' complement / ten's complement"; prior art found and credited. Per-theorem prior-art searches — OEIS, zbMATH Open, OpenAlex, Crossref, arXiv — are recorded, with what was searched, where and when, in the living ledger src/proof/novelty.json (main branch). No novelty is claimed here.

The theorems.

  1. the_reflection_is_an_involution — digits.all (fun d => refl (refl d) == d) record
  2. one_side_is_reflected_onto_itself — tetB.all (fun d => tetB.contains (refl d)) record
  3. the_other_two_swap — tetA.all (fun d => axis.contains (refl d)) ∧ axis.all (fun d => tetA.contains (refl d)) record
  4. exactly_one_digit_is_unmoved — (digits.filter (fun d => refl d == d)) = [5] record
  5. exactly_one_digit_reflects_out_of_range — (digits.filter (fun d => refl d > 9)) = [0] ∧ refl 0 = 10 record
  6. the_classes_partition_the_nine — tetA.length + tetB.length + axis.length = 9 ∧ (tetA ++ tetB ++ axis).eraseDups.length = 9 ∧ digits.length = 10 record
  7. every_digit_is_sorted_exactly_once — digits.all (fun d => (tetB.contains d && tetB.contains (refl d)) || (tetA.contains d && axis.contains (refl d)) || (axis.contains d && tetA.contains (refl d)) || (refl d == d) || (refl d > 9)) record
  8. the_fall_fixes_every_digit_but_the_void — (digits.filter (fun d => fall d != d)) = [0] ∧ nonzero.all (fun d => fall d == d) record
  9. the_fall_and_the_reflection_share_one_exceptional_digit — (digits.filter (fun d => fall d != d)) = (digits.filter (fun d => refl d > 9)) record
  10. on_the_fixed_points_the_reflection_never_leaves — nonzero.all (fun d => refl d >= 1 && refl d <= 9) ∧ nonzero.all (fun d => refl (refl d) == d) record
  11. what_escapes_falls_back_inside — refl 0 = 10 ∧ fall 10 = 1 ∧ nonzero.contains (fall 10) record
  12. the_nines_complement_pairs_the_ten_digits — digits.all (fun d => digits.contains (9 - d) && 9 - (9 - d) == d && 9 - d != d) ∧ (digits.filter (fun d => d < 9 - d)).length * 2 = digits.length record
